author: Falk
name_in_asr: Nābhika 那毗伽, birthplace of Krakucchanda; Gotihawa
asr_identification: Gotihawa, Kapilvastu district, Nepal
evidence: Faxian's route: 12 yojanas (c. 120 km at c. 10 km/yojana) SE of Śrāvastī to Krakucchanda's town; at Gotihawa the lower part of an Aśokan pillar stands in situ, and it is not the lower part of the Nigliwa pillar; Xuanzang reports an Aśokan pillar there.
quote: This birthplace was not unreasonably identiied with the present-day hamlet called Gotihawa in Nepal, since it still holds the lower part of an Aśokan pillar in situ,9 which is deinitely not the lower part of the pillar at Nigliwa on which another of the former Buddhas, konāgamana, is mentioned.
note: Agrees with the study's Gutiva (Gotihawa) and adds Falk's yojana test from Śrāvastī. It is tested in Faxian's frame, not on Xuanzang's 50 li S of the city. Mizutani names no site.

author: Falk
asr_identification: Gotihawa, Nepal (Verardi's excavation)
evidence: After Verardi 2007: the site is old enough but nothing proves the identification; the pillar was brought down already in the 3rd century AD; the stūpa rests directly on an older habitation level; its Mauryan level is 19.5 m across, with triangular bricks; enlarged to 22 m (post-Mauryan to 2nd century AD); TL dates on the bricks allow c. 280 BC; Waddell found the stūpa empty.
quote: the site is old enough to be the birthplace of a pre-Buddhist saint but that there is no deinite proof for an identiication. The pillar was brought down already in the third century a.d. (Verardi 2007: 131b)…Verardi (2007: 128) trusts Tl data for the Gotihawa bricks, which would make 280 b.c. possible.
note: Adds site evidence for 06.02.05 (excavated Mauryan stūpa beside the in-situ pillar stump), which matches Xuanzang's relic stūpa with a pillar. But if the pillar fell in the 3rd century, Xuanzang's standing 30-ft lion pillar is old report, as Falk says ('Xuanzang again seems to accumulate older material'). The study's confidence (low) could rise only within the Tilaurakot frame.

author: Falk
asr_identification: Taulihawa, Kapilvastu district, Nepal: temple whose linga is a piece of the Gotihawa pillar
evidence: After Khadga Shumsher Rana 1904 (in Joshi and Joshi 1996): a larger piece of the upper part of the Gotihawa Aśokan pillar is used as a linga in the temple at Taulihawa.
quote: For a larger piece of the upper part of the pillar being used as a linga in the temple at Taulihawa cf. khadga Shumsher rana 1904 in Joshi and Joshi 1996: 63f.
note: Falk does not link the temple to Xuanzang. If this is the Tauleshvara temple of the study's 06.02.x10, its cult object is a reused pillar fragment, not an old stone image, which weakens the match with Xuanzang's Īśvara temple. Not in Mizutani.

author: Falk
asr_identification: find-place of the Nigliwa (Nigali Sagar) pillar, 10 km NE of Gotihawa, Nepal; original site uncertain
evidence: Faxian's 1 yojana from Krakucchanda's town matches the 10 km from Gotihawa to the pillar's find-place; whether it stands where Aśoka set it up is uncertain. The inscription: Aśoka raised the Konāgamana stūpa 'a second time' in his 14th year (Falk: rebuilt in burnt brick over an earthen mound) and came in his 20th year and set up the pillar.
quote: The actual ind-place of a broken Aśokan pillar mentioning a memorial site of this former Buddha lies 10 km north-east from Gotihawa, perfectly answering the single yojana, but it remains uncertain as to whether this ind-place is close to the site of the pillar’s original erection…Aśoka in his 14th regnal year raised the stūpa of koṇāgamana “a second time”
note: Agrees with Mizutani's and the study's cautious formulation (near the pillar if in situ). The NE bearing from Gotihawa also fits Xuanzang's 30-odd li NE of Krakucchanda's town. Adds no stūpa found near the pillar.

author: Falk
asr_identification: E of Nigliwa, not Tilaurakot; Piprahwa (Siddharthnagar, UP)
evidence: Distance test on Faxian: from Gotihawa 10 km N to Konāgamana's town (Nigliwa), then less than 10 km E to Kapilavastu. Tilaurakot lies between Gotihawa and Nigliwa, so Faxian would have passed it; his Kapilavastu lay further E.
quote: Faxian went north from Gotihawa, 10 km, to see the hometown of koṇāgamana, and from there he went east for less than ten km to kapilavastu. Since Tilaurakoṭ is situated between Gotihawa and Nigliwa, he could have passed it on his way to koṇāgamana. Instead, he had to move further east from Nigliwa for the capital, so that Tilaurakoṭ was not the kapilavastu shown to him.
note: Against Mizutani's Tilaurakot for Faxian's city; agrees with the study's Piprahwa–Ganwaria. It tests Faxian, not Xuanzang, whose order is the reverse (city, then Krakucchanda 50 li S, then Kanakamuni 30 li NE). Falk himself notes the 'east' from Nigliwa really needs 'south-east' (p. 46).

author: Falk
asr_identification: Piprahwa preferred to Tilaurakot
evidence: Xuanzang may not have visited Kapilavastu and may have culled earlier reports (no other Tang pilgrim visits Lumbinī or Kapilavastu). Taking Watters' summary that both pilgrims put Lumbinī 9–10 miles (14.5–16 km) E of Kapilavastu: Piprahwa is 15 km W of Lumbinī, Tilaurakot 25 km NW.
quote: Xuanzang’s text is a repository of uncertainties, and he may not have visited kapilavastu at all but culled the details from earlier reports…Piprahwa lies 15 km straight west of lumbinī, and Tilaurakoṭ 25 km north-west, so another point for Piprahwa.
note: Agrees with the study. But the test uses Watters' summary, not Xuanzang's own figures (Arrow Well 30 li SE of the Nyagrodha grove, Lumbinī 80–90 li NE of it), which the route test of the study treats directly; the doubt that Xuanzang went there at all is Falk's and new to the study.

author: Falk
asr_identification: Piprahwa, close to Kapilavastu; palace area not found
evidence: The Piprahwa monastery's sealings read devaputra-vihāre kapilavastu-bhikhu-saṃghe (Srivastava 1979 pls. 6–7; 1996 pls. XLVII-A, XLVIII-B). Falk dates the script as 'of a Gupta type', the Kushan name of the vihāra being recent: c. 700 years after the Buddha. Mani and Mishra 2013: the Buddhist compounds at Piprahwa do not stand on city ground.
quote: There is a place which deinitely was close to kapilavastu, and that is Piprahwa…The script is of a Gupta type, and the name of the monastery shows that the time of the kushans had not passed long ago…the Buddhist compounds at Piprahwa did not occupy city ground and so the search for the palace area of kapilavastu can continue.
note: Supports the study's reading of the sealings (a Kapilavastu monks' community, not the city). Differs on date: Falk's Gupta-type script is later than IAR 1972–73's 'first-second century A.D.', which brings the sealings closer to Faxian, not to Xuanzang. Mani and Mishra 2013 (not in the study) find no city at Piprahwa itself, so the palace (06.02.x2) stays open.

author: Falk
asr_identification: Tilaurakot, Nepal: a nigama (trading post / caravan station), not shown to be the Buddha's Kapilavastu
evidence: Burnt brick is no older than Aśoka, so the visible walls cannot be the Buddha's; two clay tokens from the walled compound read negameye in early Brāhmī (Rijal 1979: 37; Coningham's team 2016), i.e. 'one living in the nigama', a trading post; the compound would suit a caravan station.
quote: the wide use of burnt bricks is only as old as Aśoka, so the presently visible vestiges cannot date back to the…We have two tokens in burnt clay from this compound, one unearthed by rijal (1979: 37), reading negameye in a circular arrangement in Brāhmī script…this latter is a term for a trading post.
note: Against Mizutani's Tilaurakot; supports the study's choice. The negameye tokens are new to the study. Falk grants that nigamas could later become state centres, so they do not exclude Tilaurakot as the city Xuanzang was shown in the 7th century.

author: Falk
asr_identification: Piprahwa
evidence: Zhi Sengzai's Wai-guo-shi (in the Shuijing zhu, before AD 420) reports a ruined Kapilavastu where a king repaired one stūpa with help from the king of Ceylon; Falk takes the king for a Kushan (Kaniṣka or Huviṣka) and matches the Kushan-period enlargement of the Piprahwa stūpa (smaller bricks, 22.4 m drum, 23.5 m platform; Kaniṣka and Huviṣka coins at Ganwaria). Tilaurakot has no stūpa repaired in Kushan times.
quote: Presupposing that the memory of the relics from lumbinī interred at Piprahwa was kept alive up to the kushans, the report of the yuezhi monk preserved in the River Classic Commentary makes good sense, speaking again for Piprahwa as kapilavastu and against Tilaurakot which to my knowledge has no stūpa repaired in kushan times.
note: Agrees with the study; the Wai-guo-shi passage is new to it. Its date (before 420) again bears on Faxian's Kapilavastu, not on Xuanzang's.

author: Falk
asr_identification: Piprahwa stūpa: the Śākyas' enshrinement of Buddha relics
evidence: Defends the Peppé casket inscription as genuine (the 'Siam conspiracy' doubts rest on the copies). Reads nidhāna as the enshrinement: the whole stūpa installed by Śākyas for the Buddha's relics. Palaeography (Aśokan bha, dha, ya, side anusvāra; Māgadhī l for r, -e) puts it before Bharhut, late 3rd century BC; the first stūpa with the base chambers and the coffer c. 200 BC; Kushan enlargement later.
quote: Thus we can say that the Piprahwa text should be older than Bharhut, and a time of origin in the later part of the third century b.c. is not at all impossible…“this whole stūpa construction has been installed by us Śākyas for the relics of the Buddha.”
note: Adds to the study's Piprahwa case: an early inscription naming the Śākyas (not Kapilavastu) at the stūpa. Falk holds that the stūpa is younger than those of Krakucchanda and Konāgamana and that its coffer and crystal reliquary came from Aśoka's installation at Lumbinī.

author: Falk
asr_identification: Ganwaria, 1 km SW of Piprahwa: two monasteries, burnt c. AD 300
evidence: Ganwaria, 1 km SW of Piprahwa, has two more monasteries (Piprahwa three, one the Kapilavastu-vihāra); after Srivastava (1996: 25) the monasteries at Ganwaria were destroyed by fire around AD 300, the end of the Buddhist communities in the area.
quote: Piprahwa has much better cards, housing a kapilavastu-vihāra amongst the three monasteries still visible today, and it has another large place, Ganwaria with another two monasteries…The end of the Buddhist communities in the area is documented by the forceful destruction by ire of the monasteries at Ganwaria
note: Differs from Srivastava's reading of the Ganwaria complexes as Śuddhodana's palace and a 'school', which the study keeps as alternatives for 06.02.x2 and 06.02.x6: Falk calls them monasteries. A destruction c. AD 300 means nothing there was standing in use for Xuanzang (and the study notes no level after the 4th century).

author: Falk
asr_identification: Rummindei (Lumbini), Nepal
evidence: Aśoka's Rummindei inscription makes the village aṭhabhāgiya ('sharing in the eight parts'): Falk reads that Aśoka brought a portion of the relics there; there is no Aśokan stūpa at Lumbinī, but a small cubical brick structure there held a reliquary. Falk proposes that the Piprahwa coffer (Pabhosa sandstone, Aśokan workmanship) and crystal reliquary first stood at Lumbinī and were moved 15 km to Piprahwa after the Mauryas.
quote: He freed the village of all taxes and made it aṭhabhāgiya, that is Skt. āṣṭabhāgika, “connected with the eight parts,”…has to mean that he brought a morsel of the Buddha’s bones back to his birthplace (Falk 2012)…In fact, there is no Aśokan stūpa anywhere at lumbinī.
note: Agrees with Mizutani and the study (Rummindei). The relic reading and the coffer hypothesis are Falk's own; they do not move the place.

author: Falk
asr_identification: the large stūpa S of Parāsi Bazar (Ramgram, Nawalparasi, Nepal)
evidence: Faxian's 5 yojanas (c. 50 km) E of Lumbinī; the Parāsi stūpa, 'today promoted as Rāmagrāma', is 40 km from Lumbinī; the stūpa is encircled by a river (cf. the Mahāvaṃsa: the Rāmagrāma stūpa split by a flood); it yielded neither bones nor reliquaries. Excavated by S. R. Shrestha (Ancient Nepal 1999–2006) without touching the core.
quote: Five yojanas, or 50 more km, lead to rāmagrāma, the centre of the koliya clan. A large stūpa south of Parāsi Bazar, today promoted as rāmagrāma,10 is 40 km away from lumbinī and would roughly answer the requirements…the rāmagrāma stūpa stands encircled by a river
note: Differs from Mizutani's and the study's Dharmauli (open): a surveyed and excavated brick stūpa at Parāsi, not in the study's sources (new candidate). Xuanzang's 200-odd li E of Lumbinī (c. 90 km at Falk's 440 m/li) is longer than 40 km; his brick stūpa with a nāga pond beside it would fit a stūpa by water.

author: Falk
name_in_asr: place where the future Buddha abandoned his servant and horse
asr_identification: not located: 3 yojanas (c. 30 km) E of Rāmagrāma by Faxian
evidence: Placed only by Faxian's 3 yojanas E of Rāmagrāma; no site named.
quote: 30 km more to the east the place was met where the future Buddha abandoned his servant and horse and continued alone and on foot.
note: No site; agrees with the study's 'unidentified'. On Falk's frame it would lie c. 30 km E of Parāsi; Xuanzang has it 100-odd li E of the Śrāmaṇera monastery.

author: Falk
asr_identification: Rampurwa (Pipariyā), West Champaran, Bihar: the two Aśokan pillars
evidence: Sum of Faxian's yojana distances from Gotihawa to the charcoal stūpa = 120 km, which reaches Rampurwa, where two Aśokan pillars (lion capital with Pillar Edicts; bull) survive in full beside two conical earth mounds (Garrick 1883: nothing ancient found in them). The local village name is Pipariyā (the name Rampurwa was unknown locally), matching Pipphalivana; two pillars at an out-of-the-way place would be explained by the charcoal stūpa and the Mauryas' ancestral home (peacocks on the lion pillar's top).
quote: Once we start counting only from Gotihawa, the sum of distances given in yojanas is 120 km, a distance that would bring us to the Aśokan site called rampurwa, the only place where two of the Aśokan pillars have survived in full…ancient Pipphali-vana is positioned by Faxian where modern Pipariyā is found, and both would linguistically make a nice pair
note: Differs from the study's tentative Lauriya-Nandangarh and Carlleyle's Rajdhani, and from Mizutani (no site): a new candidate. Falk himself calls the name argument weak and the identification conditional ('if considered as justified'); the Rampurwa mounds held no relics. It rests on Faxian, whom Falk thinks did not go there.

author: Falk
evidence: Falk sets Xuanzang aside: he 'seems to misinterpret Faxian' and puts the charcoal stūpa an undefined distance SW of Kuśinagara.
quote: Xuanzang, as so often, is of no help as he seems to misinterpret Faxian and has the charcoal stūpa an undeined distance south-west of kuśinagara
note: Bears on the study: in Xuanzang the Nyagrodha grove is reached 180–190 li SE of the tonsure stūpa and Kuśinagara lies NE of it through forest, so Rampurwa, NE of Kasia, contradicts Xuanzang's bearing. Falk's Rampurwa is a Faxian identification, not one for 06.03.04.

author: Falk
name_in_asr: the place where the licchavis were left behind (Faxian); Allakappa
asr_identification: Lauriya Ararāj (Arraraj), East Champaran, Bihar: Aśokan pillar
evidence: Faxian: 12 yojanas from Kuśinagara to where the Licchavis were left behind, marked by an inscribed stone pillar (Deeg 2005 §88); Kuśinagara to Ararāj is 80 km, perhaps longer by ferries; Ararāj has a huge Aśokan pillar. Falk also equates the local name Arra with Pali Allakappa.
quote: Next, he speaks of another 12 yojanas to the place where the licchavis were left behind by the Buddha when he was on his last journey. Faxian describes the site as marked by a stone pillar with a legend on it (Deeg 2005: p. 545, § 88). The distance between kuśinagara and Araraj is 80 km
note: New candidate for the study's unidentified 07.03.12 (Mizutani: no site, noting Faxian's pillar). Xuanzang puts the parting place only 50–60 li NW of Vaiśālī; Lauriya Ararāj lies roughly 75 km NW of Basarh, so the match holds for Faxian's figures, not Xuanzang's.

author: Falk
name_in_asr: stūpa of Droṇa containing his kumbha
asr_identification: the great stūpa at Lauriya Nandangarh, West Champaran, Bihar (tentative)
evidence: The Nandangarh stūpa (2 km SW of the Aśokan pillar) contained a smaller stūpa beside which lay a copper vessel with an inscribed but undocumented birch-bark sheet (van Lohuizen-de Leeuw 1956).
quote: It is tempting to link the stūpa of Droṇa containing his kumbha with the huge stūpa at lauriya Nandangarh…which contained a smaller stūpa by the side of which was a “copper vessel” containing a sheet of birch-bark
note: Only 'tempting', in a footnote. Differs from the study's Bhagwanganj/Chirand for 07.02.04: Xuanzang puts the vessel stūpa 100-odd li SE of the Āṭavaka stūpa in Zhanzhu (Ghazipur region), far from Champaran. It also takes Nandangarh away from the study's tentative 06.03.04.

author: Falk
asr_identification: Kasia
note: Repeats the accepted Kasia; used only as a fixed point (111 km from Piprahwa). Agrees with Mizutani and the study.

author: Davis et al.
asr_identification: Tilaurakot, Kapilvastu district, Nepal
evidence: Reports earlier sections through the rampart: Mitra 1962 (Trench TLK-1, NW rampart) dated occupation no earlier than the 3rd and probably not later than the 2nd century BC, which 'discounted Tilaurakot' as Kapilavastu; Mishra (1967 onwards, W rampart) dated a first clay rampart to the 7th–6th century BC (NBPW, PGW), a second clay rampart to 200 BC under a brick wall, and a W gateway 2nd century BC–2nd century AD.
quote: Eliciting almost immediate controversy as Mitra’s suggested third century date discounted Tilaurakot as a possible candidate for ancient Kapilavastu…He dated this phase to between the seventh and sixth centuries BCE based on finds of Northern Black Polished ware (NBPW) and Painted Grey ware (PGW).
note: Background to the study's Tilaurakot entry (Mitra, IAR 1961–62). The controversy shows the chronology was argued as a test of the Kapilavastu identification.

author: Davis et al.
asr_identification: Tilaurakot, Nepal: fortified settlement from the 6th century BCE
evidence: Trench R (2013–14) recut Mitra's trench and cut through the brick wall for the first time. OSL: cultivation 620 ± 170 BCE; transition to urban deposits 570–580 BCE; two timber palisades (720 ± 110, most likely 6th century BCE, and 560 ± 90 BCE) on a cardinal E–W alignment; clay rampart 450 ± 130 BCE, with Śuṅga-style terracotta plaques (man with parrot; Lakṣmī) in its capping and in a pit cut into it; brick wall on top, still undated.
quote: The OSL dates indicate that the perimeter of the early settlement was defined by two phases of timber palisades in the sixth century BCE, refuting Mitra’s assertion that there was no occupation in this area of the site prior to the third and second centuries BCE…with its construction dated to 450 ± 130 BCE
note: Removes the chronological objection to Tilaurakot (Mitra's 3rd-century start), so it adds evidence for Mizutani's Tilaurakot as an early city; it does not name Kapilavastu or touch Buddhist remains. Against the study's Piprahwa–Ganwaria only in that Tilaurakot is now a dated 6th-century BCE fortified town; the sealings at Piprahwa still name Kapilavastu there.

author: Davis et al.
asr_identification: Tilaurakot: an established political centre from the 6th century BCE
evidence: Conclusion: the full circuit was probably laid out c. 6th century BCE and followed by the clay rampart and brick wall; geophysics (Coningham et al. 2015) shows a grid of cardinal roads; the brick wall's date is not yet complete.
quote: Whilst the dating of the brick fortification wall at Tilaurakot is not yet complete…Tilaurakot was an established political centre with a degree of centralisation from at least the sixth century BCE onwards.
note: Strengthens the study's 'Tilaurakot the rival': a planned walled city of the Buddha's time. The brick wall, which is what Xuanzang's 'brick-built palace city' would correspond to, is undated, so the paper does not settle what stood there in the 7th century AD.

author: Singh
asr_identification: Tilaurakot, Kapilvastu district, Nepal
evidence: Reports the Nepalese/UNESCO excavations (Bidari, Coningham): urban settlement 8th–2nd century BCE, 494 punch-marked coins of pre-Mauryan and Mauryan date, iron tools, beads, terracottas, post-holes; gates, moats, streets; Tentative List 1996; nomination deferred by the World Heritage Committee in July 2025 (ICOMOS: more comparative analysis).
quote: This group has able to discover a city with signs of urban settlement spanning between eighth to second century BCE (Cuningham et al. 1-38). As claimed by Nepal, the most significant discovery is 494 punch marked coins datable to the times of pre-Mauryan and Mauryan empire
note: Secondary summary; the coin hoard and the 2025 deferral are new to the study. Supports Tilaurakot as an early city (Mizutani's site), not its name.

author: Singh
asr_identification: Tilaurakot (as matching Xuanzang)
evidence: Claims that Xuanzang travelled about 50 li from Lumbinī to Kapilavastu and placed it W of Lumbinī with walls, monasteries and stūpas, and that this matches Tilaurakot; no distances tested.
quote: Xuanzang in his travelogue “The Great Tang Dynasty Record of the Western Regions” provides far more elaborate information in which he describes traveling approximately 50 li from Lumbinī to reach Kapilavastu…These observations align almost precisely with the location and features of Tilaurakoṭ.
note: Misreports the text: Xuanzang goes from Śrāvastī to Kapilavastu and reaches Lumbinī later, via the Arrow Well (30 li SE, then 80–90 li NE); no 50 li from Lumbinī. Carries no weight against the study.

author: Singh
asr_identification: Piprahwa (religious centre) and Ganwaria (residential quarter), Siddharthnagar, UP
evidence: Reports the Peppé casket (Śākyas, Buddha relics), Srivastava's excavations (relic caskets, punch-marked coins, NBPW, rouletted ware; Mauryan to Gupta finds), Ganwaria's brick houses and drains; the objection that the remains (3rd century BC onwards) are too late; says the Indian claim puts Piprahwa within the radius of Xuanzang's account. The Kapilavastu sealings are not mentioned.
quote: There is possibility that Ganwaria might be the residential complex of Ancient Kapilavastu, on the other hand Piprahwā may be its religious center…proponents of the Indian claim argue that Piprahwā and Ganwaria fall within the plausible radius described in Xuanzang’s travelogue.
note: Agrees with the study's Piprahwa–Ganwaria as a candidate but omits the sealings, the study's main evidence; adds nothing new on site.

author: Singh
name_in_asr: Kapilavastu as a regional capital complex
asr_identification: Tilaurakot (principal palace/administrative centre) with Piprahwa and Ganwaria as parts of one complex
evidence: Argues from the three seasonal palaces of the Pāli texts (Ramma, Suramma, Subha) and the spread of sites less than 20 km apart that Kapilavastu was a regional complex: the main palace at Tilaurakot, one or two palaces at Piprahwa or Ganwaria; recommends a joint India–Nepal World Heritage nomination.
quote: there is all possibilities that one or two of these palaces were located either at Piprahwā or Ganwaria, while the principal palace or administrative centre was at Tilaurakoṭ…I am of the view that there is need for interpreting Kapilavastu not as a single entity but as a regional capital complex
note: A compromise without new evidence; it does not address Xuanzang's single city of 14–15 li or his distances. Compatible with the study's 'Tilaurakot the rival' but not a test of it.
